title: Python Vulnerability Lookup
description: Tool: Python Vulnerability Lookup. I learned that the OSV.dev open source vulnerability database has an open CORS JSON API so I had Claude Code build this HTML tool for pasting in a pyproject.toml or requirements.txt file (or name of a GitHub repo containing those) and seeing a list of all reported vulnerabilities from that API. This is an example of using AI coding tools to quickly build security utilities.
author: Simon Willison

title: Quoting Matt Webb on Architecture and Agentic Coding
description: The thing about agentic coding is that agents grind problems into dust. Give an agent a problem and a while loop and - long term - it'll solve that problem even if it means burning a trillion tokens and re-writing down to the silicon. But we want AI agents to solve coding problems quickly and in a way that is maintainable and adaptive and composable, and where every addition makes the whole stack better. While vibing, I'm looking at lines of code less than ever before, and thinking about architecture more than ever before.
author: Simon Willison (quoting Matt Webb)

title: Vibe coding SwiftUI apps is a lot of fun
description: I have a new laptop - a 128GB M5 MacBook Pro, which early impressions show to be very capable for running good local LLMs. I got frustrated with Activity Monitor and decided to vibe code up some alternative tools for monitoring performance and I'm very happy with the results. I've built two apps: Bandwidther shows network bandwidth usage and Gpuer displays GPU/memory utilization, both as menu bar apps.
author: Simon Willison

title: We Rewrote JSONata with AI in a Day, Saved $500K/Year
description: Bit of a hyperbolic framing but this looks like another case study of vibe porting, this time spinning up a new custom Go implementation of the JSONata JSON expression language. As with other vibe-porting projects the key enabling factor was JSONata's existing test suite, which helped build the first working Go version in 7 hours and $400 of token spend. The Reco team then used a shadow deployment for a week to confirm the new implementation exactly matched the behavior of the old one.
author: Simon Willison

title: My minute-by-minute response to the LiteLLM malware attack
description: Callum McMahon reported the LiteLLM malware attack to PyPI. Here he shares the Claude transcripts he used to help him confirm the vulnerability and decide what to do about it. Claude even suggested the PyPI security contact address after confirming the malicious code in a Docker container. The transcript shows how AI tools can assist with rapid security incident response.
author: Simon Willison

title: Quantization from the ground up
description: Sam Rose continues his streak of publishing spectacularly informative interactive essays, this time explaining how quantization of Large Language Models works. The post includes the best visual explanation of how floating point numbers are represented using binary digits, and covers the importance of outlier values in quantization - rare float values that are very important to model quality. Removing even a single 'super weight' can cause the model to output complete gibberish.
author: Simon Willison

title: LiteLLM Hack: Were You One of the 47,000?
description: Daniel Hnyk used the BigQuery PyPI dataset to determine how many downloads there were of the exploited LiteLLM packages during the 46 minute period they were live on PyPI. The analysis provides concrete impact numbers for the recent LiteLLM supply chain attack, helping users understand if they may have been affected by the malicious package that included a credential stealer.
author: Simon Willison

title: Thoughts on slowing the fuck down
description: Mario Zechner created the Pi agent framework used by OpenClaw, giving considerable credibility to his opinions on current trends in agentic engineering. He's not impressed: We have basically given up all discipline and agency for a sort of addiction, where your highest goal is to produce the largest amount of code in the shortest amount of time. He argues this approach creates cognitive debt and isn't sustainable for serious software development.
author: Simon Willison

title: Auto mode for Claude Code
description: Really interesting new development in Claude Code today as an alternative to --dangerously-skip-permissions: Claude Code introduces auto mode, a new permissions mode where Claude makes permission decisions on your behalf, with safeguards monitoring actions before they run. Those safeguards appear to be implemented using Claude Sonnet 4.5 to analyze and approve or reject actions.
author: Simon Willison

title: Package Managers Need to Cool Down
description: Today's LiteLLM supply chain attack inspired me to revisit the idea of dependency cooldowns, the practice of only installing updated dependencies once they've been out in the wild for a few days to give the community a chance to spot if they've been subverted. This recent piece by Andrew Nesbitt reviews the current state of dependency cooldown mechanisms across different packaging tools including npm, pip, deno, and uv.
author: Simon Willison

title: Malicious litellm_init.pth in litellm 1.82.8 — credential stealer
description: The LiteLLM v1.82.8 package published to PyPI was compromised with a particularly nasty credential stealer hidden in base64 in a litellm_init.pth file. The package was live for 46 minutes before being removed, and analysis shows approximately 47,000 downloads occurred during that window. This highlights ongoing security challenges in the Python package ecosystem.
author: Simon Willison

title: Streaming experts
description: I wrote about Dan Woods' experiments with streaming experts the other day, the trick where you run larger Mixture-of-Experts models on hardware that doesn't have enough RAM to fit the entire model by instead streaming the necessary expert weights from SSD for each token that you process. Five days ago Dan was running Qwen3-72B-Instruct-GPTQ and has now successfully tested it with Qwen3-110B, achieving 2.3 tokens/second on a 64GB M2 MacBook Pro.
author: Simon Willison

title: Quoting Christopher Mims on AI Control
description: I really think 'give AI total control of my computer and therefore my entire life' is going to look so foolish in retrospect that everyone who went for this is going to look as dumb as Jimmy Fallon holding up a picture of his Bored Ape. Christopher Mims, Technology columnist at The Wall Street Journal, expresses skepticism about giving AI agents autonomous control over computing systems.
author: Simon Willison (quoting Christopher Mims)

title: Quoting Neurotica on AI Slop
description: Slop is something that takes more human effort to consume than it took to produce. When my coworker sends me raw Gemini output he's not expressing his freedom to create, he's disrespecting the value of my time. This quote highlights the quality concerns around AI-generated content and the social implications of uncritically sharing raw AI output.
author: Simon Willison (quoting Neurotica)

title: Quoting David Abram on AI-Assisted Programming
description: I have been doing this for years, and the hardest parts of the job were never about typing out code. I have always struggled most with understanding systems, debugging things that made no sense, designing architectures that wouldn't collapse under heavy load, and making decisions that would save months of pain later. This perspective emphasizes that AI assistance changes the programming challenge from syntax to system design and architecture.
author: Simon Willison (quoting David Abram)
